ctx.x: So anyway, I joined Duke, and from staying with Cab Calloway and the way his band was run, the first night, we opened up at the Shea Buffalo Auditorium --

or, no, it was the City Auditorium in Buffalo, New York, and we opened up with something like 7 pieces, and there was Duke sitting up there with a big smile on his face just like nothing happened, and I'm about to blow my top, because in Calloway's band, this did not happen.

items.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: I mean Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Roy Eldridge and these people, they’ll tell you right off hand, I play music.

ctx.x: Yeah. Well see I mean my conception, and I was the youngest one in all the bands I worked in, so I never was a teenager. I spent all my time with older musicians, I mean all my time was spent with older musicians. So I got many a stories and I heard of many a stories and like I mean I used to hang out with Eubie Blake you know. I mean Eubie Blake was old enough to be my grandfather, I mean great grandfather. But that’s who I hung out with. And right now, even now, I mean I meet people that’s my age group, and I…

musicians did. And I mean even today, like the older musicians I know, it was an insult to call them a jazz musician. I mean Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Roy Eldridge and these people, they’ll tell you right off hand, I play music. Don’t label me no jazz musician, ‘cause I can, where I mean with me I have played Bar Mitzvahs, I’ve played Polkas, I’ve played Waltzes, I’ve played Tangos, I mean you name it, I’m prostituted, long as you gonna pay me I’ll play. So I mean don’t label me a jazz musician. I’m a…
But now, the term now has become a compliment.
